question.:question/problem:
The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,0)$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(2r,\frac{7\pi}{6})$. Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(7,0)$.

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{(7)^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{49} \\   & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(2\cdot(7),\frac{7\pi}{6})=(14,\frac{7\pi}{6}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\   & =14\cdot\operatorname{cos}(\frac{7\pi}{6}) \\   & =14\cdot(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\   & =-7\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\   & =14\cdot\operatorname{sin}(\frac{7\pi}{6}) \\   & =14\cdot(-\frac{1}{2}) \\   & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-7\sqrt{3},-7).$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =25\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =25\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{2}\end{aligned}

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{25}{2}).$
